Nuclear power plants (NPPs), solar photovoltaics (PVs) and wind power plants (WPs) are commercial technologies, which with available hydroelectric power plants provide decarbonized electricity generation. In addition, the application of small modular reactors (SMRs) emerges, which contributes to the technological and economical diversification and completness of the nuclear energy utilization. A comparative techno-economic analysis of the deployment of large scale NPP, SMRs, as well as PVs and WPs plants was performed, whereas it is assumed that the natural resources for the new hydro plants are mainly exhausted. The construction of one 1200 MW NPP or the construction of four identical SMRs with a unit capacity of 300 MW is considered. The same amount of electricity of 9.6 TWh could be generated with a total PVs power of 3033 MW and WPs with 1706 MW, with respective load factors of 18% and 32% for the area of Serbia. Since the production of solar and wind energy is time-dependent, a mature and economically most acceptable construction of a pumped hydropower energy storage (PHES) plant with a capacity of 620 GWh is considered for the electricity accumulation. The analysis is based on the current investment costs, nuclear fuel costs, operation, maintenance and decommissioning costs, construction time and service life. The obtained results show that for a period of operation of 60 years, SMRs provide the highest Net Present Value (NPV), while the lowest value is obtained for the project that includes PVs and WPs with PHES. At a favorable discount rate of 3%, but the lowest electricity price of 80 MWh/$, the pay-back period is 35 and 40 years, respectively, for SMRs and large scale NPP, while at the same discount rate and price of 120 MWh/$, the pay-back period of these nuclear power plants is shortened to 20 and 23 years, respectively. At a discount rate of 8%, the NPV is negative both for nuclear power plants and PVs and WPs with PHES. The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) is the lowest for SMRs. The LCOE ranges from 67 $/MWh for SMRs and NPP 1200 MW at the discount rate of 3%, and up to 135 $/MWh for the NPP 1200 MW and PVs and WPs with storage at the discount rate of 8%.

Hydraulic turbines are essential components for energy generation, and their reliable operation is crucial for minimizing downtime and maintenance costs. This study introduces a real-time health monitoring system for hydraulic turbines, utilizing long short-term memory autoencoders (LSTM-AEs) to detect anomalies in vibration time-series data. To reduce the incidence of false alarms, both supervised and unsupervised learning methods were examined. The supervised LSTM-AE, trained on historical vibration data, demonstrated superior performance with an accuracy of 100% and a precision of 99% in identifying abnormal conditions. In contrast, the unsupervised LSTM-AE achieved an accuracy of 90% and a precision of 65%, indicating a lower discriminatory capability. The selected model was integrated into the LabVIEW platform to facilitate real-time anomaly detection, providing continuous monitoring through an intuitive graphical interface. A data point is classified as abnormal if its reconstruction error surpasses a predefined threshold, and an alert is generated if more than half of the samples within a sequence are identified as abnormal. These results underscore the effectiveness of supervised learning in industrial anomaly detection and support predictive maintenance strategies that enhance the reliability and sustainability of hydropower systems.

River development for hydropower, irrigation, navigation and flood control has expanded rapidly worldwide, fundamentally reshaping riverine ecosystems. Although such developments deliver critical economic and social benefits, energy generation, water supply, and agricultural productivity, they simultaneously impose severe ecological consequences. Alterations to hydrological regimes, sediment transport, water quality and habitat connectivity have particularly affected migratory fish, which depend on longitudinal river connectivity to complete their life cycles. Large dams fragment river networks, disrupt migration routes and reduce access to essential spawning and feeding habitats, thereby threatening fisheries productivity and biodiversity.
To mitigate these impacts, fish passage structures, such as fish ladders, are increasingly incorporated into hydropower projects. These facilities aim to restore ecological connectivity and enable fish migration across barriers. However, their effectiveness, particularly in tropical river systems, remains poorly understood. Most empirical evaluations have focused on temperate regions with established monitoring frameworks, leaving significant knowledge gaps in tropical rivers such as the Mekong River. This gap is critical given that tropical rivers, though among the most biodiverse and productive on Earth, are also the most vulnerable to hydropower expansion.
The Mekong River, the world’s twelfth longest river system, supports an estimated 1,200–2,000 fish species, approximately one-fifth of which are long-distance migrants. These associated fisheries are central to regional livelihoods, providing up to 80% of animal protein in riparian communities. Yet the proliferation of dams—two operational on the mainstream and more than 120 on tributaries—poses a serious threat to ecological integrity and fish migration.
This thesis examines the potential application of Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tagging for evaluating fish passage performance in tropical river systems. Research was undertaken at the Xayaburi Hydropower Plant (XHPP) in Lao PDR—a run-of-river facility with a capacity of 1,285 MW and a maximum head of 39 metres—equipped with a large-scale fish ladder. The study aimed to (1) develop and validate a PIT antenna system suitable for tropical field conditions; (2) assess the biological impacts of PIT tag implantation on native Mekong species; and (3) investigate migration dynamics and environmental drivers using multi-year monitoring data.
An optimized antenna system was designed, constructed and field-tested at XHPP. The final configuration achieved a 99.6% detection rate for 23-millimetre PIT tags under operational flow conditions. Controlled laboratory experiments demonstrated that PIT tagging produced negligible mortality and no adverse behavioural effects across four representative Mekong species, confirming its suitability for tropical fish. Analysis of four years of detection data revealed species-specific migration patterns: Hemibagrus filamentus (local name in Lao: Pa Kod-rueng), Hypsibarbus lagleri (local name in Lao: Pa Pak), and Barbonymus schwanenfeldii (local name in Lao: Pa Vien-fai) ascended the ladder in response to increasing discharge, whereas Sikukia gudgeri (local name in Lao: Pa Mang) and Puntioplites falcifer (local name in Lao: Pa Sa-kang) migrated independently of flow variation. Some species exhibited inverse relationships with temperature, highlighting the complex cues underlying tropical fish movement. Notably, H. lagleri exhibited both migratory and resident behaviours, underscoring the need for passage designs accommodating diverse life histories.
This thesis advances understanding of fish passage monitoring in tropical rivers by refining PIT technology for large, hydraulically dynamic systems and providing the first long-term dataset of Mekong fish movements through a mainstream hydropower facility. The findings offer practical insights into antenna engineering, tagging methodology and environmental response analysis, contributing directly to the design and evaluation of effective fish passage solutions in the Mekong and other tropical basins.

To address multi-source uncertainty and the accumulation of deviations between day-ahead scheduling and intraday operation in wind–solar–cascade hydropower dispatch under high wind and photovoltaic penetration, this paper proposes a dynamically corrected multi-timescale coordinated scheduling strategy. The proposed strategy coordinates wind, solar, and hydropower resources through multi-scenario optimization in the day-ahead stage and rolling re-dispatch in the intraday stage. In the day-ahead stage, K-means clustering is used to generate representative scenario sets, optimize generation schedules, and allocate reserve capacity. In the intraday stage, the dynamic correction strategy adjusts the dispatch plan based on real-time data to improve consistency with actual operating conditions. In addition, root mean square propagation (RMSprop) and stochastic alternating direction method of multipliers (SADMM) are introduced to solve the proposed multi-timescale scheduling model for the wind–solar–cascade hydropower system. Case study results show that, in the High-flow period, compared with the conventional stochastic scheduling scheme, the proposed scheme reduces the daily total cost by 14.76%, increases the wind and solar power accommodation rate by 2.89%, and reduces the fluctuation rate of hydropower output by 55.81%. Compared with the deterministic scheduling scheme, the daily total cost and hydropower output fluctuation rate are reduced by 12.67% and 64.98%, respectively. In the low-flow period, compared with the conventional stochastic scheduling scheme, the daily total cost, external electricity purchase cost, and hydropower output fluctuation rate are reduced by 19.80%, 40.14%, and 51.64%, respectively. Moreover, RMSprop–SADMM shortens the solution time by 36.95% compared with the conventional stochastic scheduling scheme, demonstrating the economic performance, operational stability, and applicability of the proposed method for intraday rolling dispatch.

Significance The upper Yangtze River waterway is a core inland navigation corridor supporting the Chengdu–Chongqing Twin-City Economic Circle and the national Western Development Strategy. It undertakes more than 70% of freight transport between the upper and middle-lower reaches of the Yangtze River and constitutes a key component of China's high-grade waterway network. Meanwhile, the upper Yangtze River serves as a critical national ecological security barrier, responsible for water conservation, biodiversity maintenance, and aquatic ecosystem stability. However, the expansion and upgrading of the waterway are constrained by the superposition of complex river regimes, cascade reservoir operation, and ecologically sensitive areas. Dense braided reaches, swift-shallow-hazardous shoals, sharply reduced sediment transport, and increasingly frequent extreme climate events jointly lower navigation reliability. Furthermore, cascade reservoirs have altered natural hydrological processes and material-energy transport, leading to reserialization of key habitats, declined longitudinal connectivity, and degradation of fish resources. The traditional governance paradigm that prioritizes navigation capacity improvement and relies on passive ecological compensation can hardly meet the requirements of high-quality and green development. Therefore, exploring the synergistic pathway between waterway construction and ecological protection is of great theoretical significance and engineering value for enhancing navigation stability, protecting rare and endemic fish, restoring riverine habitats, and realizing the sustainable development of the Yangtze River golden waterway.Progress Against the background of engineering practice and policy constraints, this study systematically proposes an integrated pathway of theory, technology, and governance for ecological waterway construction in the upper Yangtze River. In terms of theoretical research, a theoretical framework for ecological waterways is constructed with material transport and food-web dynamics as the main thread. A coupled modeling method of hydrodynamic-sediment processes, channel evolution, and ecological responses is adopted to reveal the adaptive adjustment mechanism of waterway and ecosystem under changing environments such as cascade operation and climate change. In terms of technological innovation, coordinated technologies are developed for fairway stability regulation and habitat connectivity protection in swift-shallow-hazardous shoal groups. Key technologies include low-impact reef removal, resource utilization of dredged spoils for habitat creation, ecological reefs, ecological dam structures, and ecological revetment. These technologies aim to improve navigation conditions while protecting hydrological connectivity, material circulation, and energy exchange of critical habitats. In terms of coordinated governance, a multi-objective collaborative governance model is established under unified constraints of flood control, hydropower generation, shipping, and ecology. A joint optimal operation and adaptive management framework for cascade reservoirs is proposed to balance water use among multiple sectors. The pathway also emphasizes demonstration projects, standardized specifications, and long-term monitoring systems to promote replicable and scalable applications. Priority protection and restoration are implemented for key fish spawning grounds, confluence areas of tributaries, pebble shoals, and deep pools behind reefs, so as to enhance habitat diversity and population stability of rare and endemic fishes.Conclusions and Prospects Affected by cascade reservoirs, climate change, and human activities, the upper Yangtze River is undergoing continuous adjustments in hydrological regime, sediment transport, and habitat pattern. The traditional navigation-oriented governance model is insufficiently coordinated with ecological protection, resulting in gaps in systematic integration, technical practicability, and multi-objective coordination. The integrated theory-technology-governance pathway proposed in this study can effectively alleviate conflicts between waterway construction and ecological conservation, improve the adaptability of engineering measures to changing environments, and enhance the overall benefits of shipping, ecology, and resources. In the future, further research should be carried out in the following aspects: to strengthen the long-term observation and quantitative analysis of habitat response under altered hydrological and sediment conditions; to improve the engineering applicability and standardization of low-impact regulation technologies and habitat restoration technologies; to optimize the joint operation rules of cascade reservoirs with ecological flow as a rigid constraint; and to establish a complete monitoring, evaluation, and adaptive management system. In addition, with the rapid development of information technology, the integration of artificial intelligence, big data, and digital twin models will provide new technical means for intelligent simulation of water-sediment-ecological processes, accurate identification of ecological risks, and optimized decision-making for multi-objective scheduling. These efforts will further promote the green, intelligent, and high-quality development of ecological waterways in the upper Yangtze River and provide a scientific reference for ecological protection and coordinated governance of large river inland waterways worldwide.

The objective of this master’s thesis is to investigate the response of the 5th unit of the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydropower Plant, connected to the electrical grid through a full-scale power converter, to various disturbances occurring in the power system. The thesis analyzes the dynamic behavior of a variable-speed pumped storage hydropower unit and evaluates its influence on overall power system stability. The relevance of the topic is related to the increasing integration of renewable energy sources into modern power systems, the decreasing overall system inertia, and the growing need for fast and flexible generation sources capable of maintaining frequency and voltage stability. The thesis includes an analysis of scientific literature related to hydropower plant modeling methods, frequency control principles, reactive power regulation techniques, and the application of full-scale power converters in pumped storage hydropower plants. The operating principles of variable-speed hydropower units, synthetic inertia functions, and converter-based frequency and voltage control methods are also reviewed. Attention is given to the role of converter-connected hydropower units in maintaining power system stability under rapidly changing operating conditions. During the research, a mathematical model of the 5th unit of the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydropower Plant was developed. The model includes the hydraulic system, turbine and generator mechanical parts, a full-scale MMC-based static frequency converter, and an equivalent model of the electrical grid. The model was implemented in the MATLAB/Simulink environment and adapted for the analysis of transient processes and dynamic operating modes. Frequency control, reactive power control, and grid-side voltage regulation algorithms were implemented in the model to reproduce realistic converter and hydropower unit operation. Simulation studies of the hydropower unit operation under different disturbances were performed. The response of the unit to frequency deviations, rapidly changing system frequency, voltage dips, operating mode transitions between pumping and generating modes, and symmetrical and asymmetrical short circuits were investigated. During the simulations, active and reactive power variations, generator angular speed changes, grid-side converter currents, and voltage transients were analyzed. The ability of the converter to limit fault currents and maintain stable operation during transient and fault conditions was also evaluated. The obtained results demonstrated that a variable-speed hydropower unit connected through a full-scale converter can effectively participate in power system frequency regulation and voltage support. The simulations showed that the unit is capable of rapidly responding to system frequency deviations, providing synthetic inertia support, and smoothly changing operating modes between pumping and generation. Furthermore, the converter control system was found to effectively regulate reactive power, suppress transient oscillations, and limit fault currents during symmetrical and asymmetrical short circuits. The results confirmed that variable-speed hydropower units equipped with full-scale converters can significantly contribute to power system stability, flexibility, and secure operation under modern power system conditions with a high penetration of renewable energy sources.

Ethiopia’s electricity system is highly dependent on hydropower, making it sensitive to seasonal inflow variation and drought conditions. This study evaluates the technical, economic, and system-level potential of integrating wind power and floating photovoltaic systems at the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam reservoir to support Ethiopia’s sustainable electricity supply. Hourly meteorological data from NASA POWER were processed in MATLAB to simulate wind and FPV hourly power production. System-level impacts were evaluated in EnergyPLAN under three scenarios: a hydropower-dominated baseline, a hybrid system, and a drought scenario with reduced hydropower production. The Penman model was used to measure evaporation at the GERD reservoir. Results indicate that the hybrid system significantly increases the total share of renewable energy while enhancing grid stability. A hybrid capacity of 900 MW was identified as a suitable scale for integration with the existing GERD infrastructure, considering its connection to the national grid through 500 kV transmission lines and the 400 kV link to the nearby Beles Power Plant. The proposed wind-FPV system generates 1,705 GWh/year, with 62.3% from FPV and 37.7% from wind power. The hybrid system improves production by reducing low-output periods, hours below 1 MW decrease from 4,291 hours for FPV and 1,700 hours for wind to 589 hours for the combined system. Under drought conditions, wind–FPV integration can compensate for about 18% of the reduced hydropower generation, thereby strengthening Ethiopia’s electricity supply resilience during periods of limited water availability. The economic analysis indicates an LCOE of 53.4 USD/MWh, a positive NPV of 200 million USD, and a payback period of 7.8 years. The water-energy analysis illustrates annual evaporation of 2,324 mm/year, while the selected 0.15% FPV coverage saves 5.2 million m³ of water annually. The findings demonstrate that integrating wind and FPV with GERD hydropower is technically feasible, economically attractive, and beneficial for improving Ethiopia’s renewable generation, drought resilience, and water conservation. The study provides a scalable approach for hydropower-dependent regions facing climate-related electricity supply risks.

This thesis evaluates how much energy can be recovered from a stormwater detention basin under Danish hydraulic and climatic conditions using ultra-low-head (ULH) hydropower, and how basin design and outlet configuration influence available head, discharge and turbine operating time. A 12-year rainfall dataset from the Bellinge drainage system in Odense was modelled in Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) to simulate water levels, flooding, and pumping behaviour for the existing basin and four redesigned basin configurations. Hydropower generation was then estimated in Python using efficiency curves for three ULH turbines. The results show that hydropower performance is controlled primarily by head availability. The shallow detention basins are fundamentally limited by their 1.5 m geometric depth, which restricts the head they can develop. Although the larger basins do not experience full storage a lot and it has long emptying periods, most of this time happens at very low head, which contributes very little energy. As a result, storage volume has only a minor influence on energy production. Turbine differences are muted under shallow‑head conditions when implementing turbines made for the ULH conditions. Differences in performance become clearer with additional available head. Pumping further reduces hydropower potential by removing water at low depths, although it remains essential for flood mitigation. Overall, the shallow detention basins generate approximately 40 kWh/year, while the deeper underground basin produces around 243 kWh/year. These yields are modest and not grid‑relevant, but they are sufficient to power sensors, monitoring equipment, and other self‑sustaining stormwater infrastructure. The study concludes that ULH hydropower in Danish detention basins is technically feasible but strongly constrained by shallow geometry, outlet design, and rainfall intermittency. From a sustainability perspective, ULH hydropower can enhance the multifunctionality of climate‑adaptation infrastructure by supporting local renewable energy generation.

The Swedish energy system is undergoing major changes due to electrification and the transition from fossil fuels to fossil-free energy carriers. Electrification is expected to increase electricity use in several sectors, particularly transport, industry and new electricity-intensive activities. This places new demands on electricity production, electricity grids and flexibility. To support planning for this transition, there is a need for greater understanding of how changes in electricity use and production may affect the regional power balance, in this case in Uppsala County.T his study is intended to support the County Administrative Board of Uppsala County in developing an action plan for electrification up to 2045. The analysis is based on several scenarios describing possible development pathways for electricity use and generation in the county, including a baseline scenario, industrialisation scenarios, a resource efficient electrification scenario and a resilience scenario. Using hourly electricity use and production for 2023 as a starting point, the study examines how future electricity use, production and flexibility may affect the power balance in 2045. In the modelling, electricity use and production for the reference year 2023 were compiled using data from Svenska kraftnät, Statistics Sweden and ENTSO-E. This current system representation was then used as the basis for constructing the future scenarios. Depending on data availability and energy source, changes were represented by modifying existing time series, simulating production profiles or applying assumptions from literature studies. The power balance was analysed as the difference between electricity use and electricity production. A Vehicle-to-Grid, V2G, model was also included to examine how storage may reduce imbalances between production and electricity use. The results show that increased electrification leads to a greater need for both electricity production and flexibility in Uppsala County. In scenarios with sharply increased electricity use, especially through electricity-intensive industry, deficits increase clearly and the need for imports from the overlying electricity grid remains during large parts of the year. Although expanded electricity production can improve the annual energy balance, the results show that the timing and variability of production are also crucial for the power balance. The V2G analysis shows that storage can help even out the power balance and reduce imports and exports in some scenarios. However, its effect depends on the availability of surplus electricity that can be stored and later used during deficits. Where deficits are large and long-lasting, the contribution of storage is more limited. The resilience scenarios also show that Uppsala County remains strongly dependent on the overlying electricity grid. Local dispatchable and controllable production, such as hydropower and combined heat and power, appears particularly important for system robustness during disturbances. Overall, the study shows that Uppsala County’s future electricity system is strongly affected by the scale of electrification, electricity-intensive activities, local production expansion and access to flexibility resources. Meeting future electricity demand will require increased electricity production, more efficient electricity use, flexibility, storage and continued access to the overlying electricity system. The results can therefore support further regional energy planning and continued analysis of how Uppsala County can meet electrification in a robust and resource efficient way.

Objective. Large-scale integration of wind and photovoltaic (PV) power has significantly intensified operational uncertainties in power grids, while traditional dispatch models are still unable to accurately characterize the diversified energy consumption paths in practical power systems. Against this background, this study conducted in-depth research on the medium- and long-term dispatch of cascade hydro-wind-solar complementary systems, aiming to quantify the impacts of large-scale wind and PV integration on the operational characteristics of cascade reservoirs, reveal the intrinsic coupling mechanism between transmission channel constraints and reservoir scheduling, propose scientific and feasible coordinated dispatch strategies and reserve capacity allocation schemes that balance system security and reliable supply with efficient renewable energy accommodation, and further enhance the adaptability of the dispatch model to actual power grid structures and operational rules.Methods. Taking the Yalong River Basin hydro-wind-solar integrated base — the first national demonstration base of its kind in China — and its involved Ya'an and Panxi key transmission sections as the research object, a medium- and long-term complementary optimal dispatch model considering coordinated control of multiple transmission sections and diversified energy consumption paths was established. The model took the maximization of annual system power generation and the highest comprehensive dry-season supply capacity as the dual optimization objectives, and effectively realized the priority consumption of wind and PV power by assigning higher weight coefficients to wind and PV power than to hydropower. To ensure the rationality and practicality of the model, three-level physical constraints of the power grid, river basin, and power stations were comprehensively considered; specifically, on the power grid side, three types of consumption paths with different priority levels — local load consumption, external transmission agreements, and main grid transmission — were explicitly introduced to fit the actual dispatch logic of the power grid in southwest China. A hybrid intelligent algorithm combining Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Progressive Optimal Algorithm (POA), namely PSO-POA, was adopted for global optimal solution, which effectively balanced the solution efficiency and optimization accuracy. To fully reflect the impact of uncertainties and different grid conditions on dispatch results, two typical scenarios were set up for comparative analysis: a transmission-constrained scenario in 2024 and a transmission-expanded scenario in 2025. Meanwhile, four runoff scenarios representing wet, normal, dry, and extremely dry years were designed to characterize the uncertainty of inflow, and a control scheme with a single consumption path was also established to quantitatively verify the superiority of the proposed multi-path consumption model.Results and Discussions. The calculation results showed that the transmission channel capacity played a dominant role in determining the operational strategy of the cascade reservoirs. Under the transmission-constrained scenario, the system presented a typical regulatory operational characteristic of "leading reservoir dominance, priority impoundment in the upstream, and auxiliary discharge in the downstream". Specifically, the fullness rate and full-pool duration of Murong Reservoir (the upstream leading reservoir) were significantly increased, and the hydropower generation was reduced by 0.30%~1.40%. Through the appropriate sacrifice of hydropower benefits, the system effectively ensured the full accommodation of wind and PV power and the security of dry-season power supply. Correspondingly, the dry-season output of the Ya'an and Panxi transmission sections was increased by 15.55%~17.41% and 33.09%~46.08%, respectively. In contrast, under the transmission-unconstrained scenario, the cascade reservoirs restored the optimal operation mode of "synchronous storage and discharge, stable water level decline", and the hydropower generation was barely affected. Under this scenario, the dry-season output of the two sections was further increased by 36.91%~39.28% and 86.46%~92.69%, respectively, realizing efficient and coordinated operation of hydro, wind, and PV power. In addition, the reserve capacity allocation exhibited significant spatial priority; allocating the reserve capacity to the upstream leading reservoir first achieved the optimal comprehensive benefit, and reserving 10% of the regulating capacity was proven to be the optimal scheme, which maximized the dry-season supply capacity with minimal hydropower generation loss.Conclusions. Under high-proportion wind and solar integration, the operational strategy of cascade reservoirs is deeply coupled with transmission channel conditions and energy consumption structures. Transmission bottlenecks will force hydropower to transform from a traditional energy-type power source to a regulatory power source, which supports renewable energy accommodation and system supply security by actively adjusting its storage and discharge process. When the transmission conditions are improved, efficient coordinated optimization of hydro, wind, and PV power can be realized, and the comprehensive benefits of the system can be significantly improved. The upstream leading reservoir, with its strong regulation performance, occupies an irreplaceable advantage in reserve capacity allocation, and the reasonable reservation of reserve capacity is a key means to enhance the operational robustness of the system during the dry season. The established multi-path and multi-section dispatch model is more consistent with the actual power grid operation mechanism, and its research results can provide direct technical support for the reserve capacity allocation and medium- and long-term dispatch decision-making of the Yalong River Basin hydro-wind-solar integrated base. Furthermore, the relevant ideas and methods can be further promoted and applied to other similar hydro-wind-solar integrated bases in southwest China, which is of great practical significance and engineering application value for supporting the implementation of the "West-to-East Power Transmission" national strategy, improving the safe and stable supply capacity of the new power system, and helping the steady realization of the "dual carbon" goal.

Achieving net-zero emissions — defined as the balance between greenhouse gases (GHG) produced and the amount captured through natural sinks or engineered technologies — will require deep, systemic transformations to reduce emissions across energy, land, and economic systems (i.e., deep decarbonization). These transformations will have cascading effects on water resources and other sustainability goals. Such effects are highly region-specific, particularly in large, resource-diverse countries like Canada, where regional differences in infrastructure, resource endowments, and sectoral activity shape both water use patterns and broader socio-economic and environmental sustainability. However, provincial and regional “subnational” assessments of these dynamics remain underexplored in integrated assessment modeling frameworks. This thesis addressed this gap by integrating three research questions to assess how socioeconomic development and climate mitigation impact water use and broader sustainable development outcomes across Canada. First, a novel, consistent, spatially-disaggregated dataset of historical water withdrawals (2005–2018) was developed across seven water-use sectors to establish baseline patterns and identify their key drivers at provincial and river basin scales. Building on the resulting regional dataset, we developed a new provincially disaggregated water module within the GCAM-Canada integrated assessment model, enabling projections of future water use under a reference scenario and deep decarbonization pathways. These pathways were used to evaluate the implications of the large systemic transformations, including shifts in electricity generation, land use, and international trade on local water use. Further, we analyzed the impacts of deploying the emerging direct air capture (DAC) technology, which is highly energy- and water-intensive, on local water resources in Canada, for the first time to our knowledge. Finally, the study expanded from an assessment of “water futures” to include the broader interactions between climate mitigation policies and a set of Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), namely, food security (SDG2), water availability (SDG 6), energy accessibility and affordability (SDG7), and economic development (SDG 8). Key findings were the spatial heterogeneity of the effects of decarbonization pathways on water and other sustainability metrics across provinces, shaped by provincial differences in energy systems, the regionally dominant water withdrawing sectors, and carbon storage capacity. The analysis assessed results in terms of synergies and trade-offs between climate mitigation and sustainability outcomes. Synergies included lower water withdrawals in some regions, particularly through the phase-out of once-through cooling systems and coal-fired power, and clean renewable energy expansion and accessibility. Trade-offs included increased irrigation demands for bioenergy, greater evaporative losses from hydropower reservoirs in hydropower producing provinces, rising electricity costs in northern remote regions, and disproportionate resource burdens in provinces hosting carbon removal technologies, particularly in Western Canada. These findings emphasize the need for decarbonization policy approaches that recognize Canada’s regional diversity in energy systems, water availability, and socioeconomic conditions. This work demonstrates the value of integrated assessment models such as GCAM-Canada in assessing the systemic and regionally diverse impacts of deep decarbonization policies. While IAMs provide a powerful framework for analyzing cross-sectoral and cross-regional dynamics under climate policies and informing deep decarbonization pathways, there remains room for development, particularly in enhancing spatial and sectoral resolution to extend the range of questions they can address and the insights they can generate at subnational scales.

Swedish hydropower plays a central role in the national energy system, accounting for approximately 40 per cent of electricity generation while providing both renewable electricity and grid regulation capacity. At the same time, hydropower constitutes one of the most significant anthropogenic pressures on freshwater ecosystems, contributing to the loss of naturally free-flowing rivers. In response to these impacts, the Swedish government adopted in 2020 a national plan for the reassessment of environmental conditions for hydropower facilities, in short NAP. Spanning a twenty-year period, the plan covers almost 2,000 hydropower facilities and regulation dams. Despite the extensive scope of this process, there is currently no comprehensive, easily accessible and up-to-date overview of existing fish passages, mitigation measures (implemented or planned), or reassessment timelines. This master’s thesis aimed to map, compile and analyse information on fish passages and other environmental mitigation measures at Swedish hydropower facilities, and to develop a Geographic Information System (GIS)-based web interface that visualises the spatial distribution, status and reassessment schedule of these measures under NAP. The results demonstrate that a GIS-based web interface can function as an effective tool for analysing and visualising hydropower-related environmental measures, thereby improving accessibility and transparency for both professional stakeholders and the general public. The compiled data indicate an uneven geographical distribution of fish passages and mitigation measures, as well as substantial data gaps regarding design, function and status. Integration of reassessment data from NAP reveals that approximately 18 per cent of the 1,610 facilities required to submit applications under NAP had done so at the time of the study, and that most facilities undergoing reassessment are small-scale hydropower plants (<1.5 MW). This thesis concludes that the developed web interface should be regarded as an analytical tool at an overview level, providing insights into the spatial distribution of mitigation measures and reassessment processes while simultaneously revealing information gaps and structural challenges. The results underline the need for more standardised and coordinated environmental data to support an effective and transparent implementation of NAP.

This research provides the first comprehensive assessment of antibiotics and nutrients in Cirata reservoir, a multifunctional tropical reservoir in Indonesia, linking pollution sources to ecological risks and management strategies. The research develops a framework to evaluate the occurrence, prioritization, sources, fate, transport, and impacts of antibiotics and nutrients, and to predict their future state and proposed management strategies under different climate change and socio-economic scenarios. Twelve antibiotics were prioritized for monitoring, with livestock farming identified as the dominant source, and point sources exceeding diffuse sources. Under an economy-driven scenario with strong climate change, Cirata reservoir may face combined pressures from nutrient enrichment and antibiotic mixtures by 2050, threatening hydropower generation, aquaculture, and irrigation. Integrated management strategies addressing both nutrients and antibiotics are most effective for mitigating these risks, although nutrient-focused strategies alone can also reduce antibiotic loads. The findings provide a scientific basis for designing targeted interventions to protect reservoir ecosystem services and contribute to achieving multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Sustainability is one of the main factors driving the development of transportation. Phasing out fossil fuels and transitioning to electrified transportation is currently often seen as a step in the right direction. In this master's thesis, the objective is to investigate whether battery swapping is applicable to electric aircraft. A literature study is conducted on topics relevant to the research questions, along with a MATLAB Simulink simulation of airplanes' energy consumption during the flight mission and their total range. Current generations of batteries and the next generation of batteries are researched and simulated to provide data on how electric aviation is holding up currently and how future batteries may transform transportation in the future. Battery degradation is also considered, and the potential for repurposing degraded batteries in battery energy storage systems, after they are no longer suitable for safe flight, is discussed. Battery energy storage systems are crucial for the storage capabilities of both energy bought from the grid and green energy generated by the airport's renewable sources, potentially from photovoltaic systems, wind power, hydropower, or geothermal energy. After conducting a thorough literature study and simulations, the results indicate that metal-air batteries are the most viable option due to their high theoretical energy density. All metal-air batteries are inherently different, with some being primary batteries and others being secondary batteries, making their battery swapping capabilities vary with the metal electrode used. Future research will determine which metal-air battery is most suited for use in electric aviation, and whether it works with battery swapping or not.

Pumped storage hydropower (PSH) is a mature energy storage system having the benefits of low environmental impacts, while presenting a robust solution for integration of intermittent renewable energy generation. Comparative assessments of energy storage systems can be done using Life Cycle Assessments (LCA’s). The global warming potential (as CO2 eq g/kWh) attributed to 1kWh of renewable energy (intermittent wind and solar energy) stored in a pumped storage hydropower plant is assessed within the problem boundary of cradle to gate plus production. A 1000 MW pumped storage plant is selected to be representative of a possible design in Quebec (Bad Creek, USA providing the material inventory). Four proposed Canadian pumped storage projects of different design types and located in different provinces and the 1000 MW plant are assessed for their global warming potential in construction and operations based on local grid composition under Net Zero energy aspirations. The material requirements were estimated by modifying a materials-use-model of existing dams in the US. The LCAs were undertaken using Openlca software in conjunction with the ecoinvent v3.10 database. The global warming potential range of the pumped storage hydro projects is 32 (±12%) to 81 (±5%) g CO2-eq/kWh for storage of either solar and/or wind energy. The global warming potential has a contribution from construction and from operations of the plant. Construction contributes from 5-12% the total and operations contributes from 89-95% of the total. The main contribution from operations is due to energy loss from the round trip efficiency, typically 80% for pumped storage hydropower. The magnitude of the associated global warming potential depends on the energy stored, which should be intermittent renewable energy from wind or solar power. Note that in Quebec, the storage capacity of the hydropower reservoirs is over 100% of the annual yearly production, so pumped storage hydropower may only be needed to meet peak power demand. The global warming potential from construction is comprised of the construction of the dam for the reservoir (79 – 94%; 2-10 gCO2-eq/kWh), of the powerhouse 4-15 % (0.37 – 0.4 gCO2-eq/kWh) and of the water channels with 2-9% (0.21-0.33 gCO2-eq/kWh). LCA results for pumped storage hydropower in the literature differ due to different problem boundaries, the LCA database and software selected, but most fundamentally to the grid composition of the energy stored and its carbon cost per kWh. The aim of LCAs is ambitious, yet the current use of its results is limited, as it is a summation of inputs with limited representative local data, and it relies on available averages, which might not represent local conditions. Although LCA software has a framework for assessing environmental impacts other then global warming potential, there is, as yet, no data or accepted methodology for assessing these impacts. LCA results of global warming potential can contribute to decision making, but must be added to information assessing on the complex implications of material transformation, and include implications from human interactions, energy properties, labour requirements and project management essentials, to provide a complete technology environmental impact assessment. This is particularly key for complex facilities such as large civil engineering projects of pumped storage hydropower systems, which are unique in terms of its functionality, execution and long-term ecosystem degradation throughout its life cycle.Using LCA results, which are based on linear mass relationships with environmental factors, simplifies environmental impacts and are likely to obscure the interpretation of optimal decision-making data. If decision making is based on LCAs assessments of global warming potential due to the prominence of GHG NetZero goals, burden shifting to other pollution mechanisms is at stake.

Energy storage systems have been considered in the last few years to improve the performance of energy grids. In a typical power system, an instantaneous balance between generated and consumed power must be maintained, without storing energy. As a result, the power generation must follow the load curve, and due to the variability of electrical demand, the operation of the energy grid may not be economically efficient. Balancing total generated power with total demand, while accounting for losses, requires optimal performance of the electric power system. Consequently, one of the critical components in any energy network is its ability to regulate load frequency effectively. This study investigates the effect of an energy storage system on enhancing load frequency regulation performance in an interconnected energy network comprising two-area steam and hydropower plants. Initially, the energy grid model, incorporating a superconducting magnetic energy storage (SMES) unit, is expressed in state space using first-order differential equations. Subsequently, the effect of the energy storage system on the power network is explored through system mode analysis. Results from time-domain simulations conducted in MATLAB demonstrate the effectiveness of the system mode investigation and its responsiveness to load fluctuations, confirming the reliability of the approach.

To address the economic and risk issues of high‐proportion renewable energy power systems, a two‐layer optimal dispatch model for a cascaded hydropower–wind–solar joint system in the electricity market is proposed. The upper layer is aimed at minimizing the system cost and conditional value at risk to optimize the day‐ahead generation plan. The lower layer constructs a real‐time market leader–follower game based on the day‐ahead generation results of wind, solar, and hydropower obtained from the upper layer: the market operator (leader) maximizes social welfare through electricity price decisions; the wind–solar–hydropower alliance (follower) responds to electricity prices to optimize real‐time generation and uses the Shapley value method to allocate alliance benefits. Through closed‐loop feedback of actual generation, the risk aversion coefficient, wind and hydropower deviation penalty coefficient are dynamically and adaptively adjusted to achieve rolling optimization. The second stage builds an optimal dispatch model for the real‐time market of the wind–solar–hydropower system based on the results of the first stage, optimizing the clearing price and allocating the system′s benefits. To address the shortcomings of traditional solution algorithms in terms of accuracy and speed, an improved Mantis Shrimp Optimization Algorithm (MShOA) is proposed, introducing inertia weights, Lévy flights, and adaptive rotation angles and step sizes in foraging, attacking, and defending, respectively, to ensure population diversity and enhance the algorithm′s spatial search ability. Case studies show that the proposed model can effectively mitigate the fluctuations of renewable energy, reduce system risks, and improve economic efficiency.

The transition toward a fossil‑free Swedish energy system is expected to significantly increase electricity demand by 2050, with scenarios ranging from 250 to 350 TWh. At the same time, new generation capacity is anticipated to come primarily from wind power and nuclear power, including small modular reactors (SMRs). This thesis investigates the potential of SMRs to contribute to system flexibility and balancing in a future Swedish power system dominated by variable renewable energy, such as wind power. Four SMR designs considered most relevant for Swedish conditions, BWRX-300 developed by GE Vernova Hitachi, the Rolls-Royce SMR, the AP300 by Westinghouse, and NuScale’s SMR. These are examined with respect to their operational characteristics, particularly their ability to regulate output through load‑following operation. A power system model for the year 2050 is developed using the Python‑based framework PyPSA. Multiple scenarios are simulated to capture uncertainties in future electricity demand, generation mix, and SMR deployment levels. Historical production and load data are scaled to reflect future conditions, and the model optimizes hourly dispatch over a full year. The analysis compares constant output and load following operation of SMRs and evaluates their contribution to system balance, including relative regulation effort, import needs and system inertia. The results show that SMRs increase the relative regulation contribution from hydropower by providing stable baseload generation, thereby allowing a greater share of hydropower capacity to be used for balancing. Load‑following operation yields a notably higher regulation contribution than constant operation. The relative regulation contribution increases further in scenarios with lower electricity demand and a higher share of SMRs. However, reducing reactor output leads to lower revenues from electricity production. While participation in ancillary service markets can provide compensation for flexibility, this must be balanced against increased costs associated with flexible operation. The simulations also indicate that the geographical placement of SMRs has a substantial impact on system balance due to transmission constraints between Swedish bidding zones. In addition, SMRs provide stabilizing system services, such as inertia and voltage regulation, that are limited in wind power, suggesting that SMRs can help mitigate the increased need for frequency and voltage support in a wind-dominated system. Overall, the findings highlight that SMRs can play a meaningful role in enhancing flexibility, stability, and balancing capability in Sweden’s future electricity system, particularly when operated in a load‑following mode and strategically located within the transmission network.

This thesis investigates how the green transition and climate change affects connection to place and grief associated with ecological changes, and if and how it influences the well-being of Sámi reindeer herders in Sweden. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with six informants, this study employs a thematic analysis and uses the concepts Place attachment and Ecological grief to understand how connection to place and grief associated with ecological changes is affected by climate change and the green transition and if and how it impacts Sámi reindeer herders well-being. Findings show that their well-being is deteriorating. The changing weather causes warmer winters, unpredictable weather, and less snow which impacts the reindeer migration routes and access to food. Additionally, investments in the green transition for wind power, forestry, and hydropower have led to exploitation of Sámi lands, which have changed the reindeers’ behavior and migrations routes. These changes have fragmentized Sámi reindeer herders' transmission of knowledge that has been used for generations. These new challenges have led to adaptations that are impacting their cultural way of life and livelihood, causing emotional distress, worry and a deteriorating well-being.

Access to reliable and sustainable electricity is fundamental for economic and social development. Zambia, like many Sub-Saharan African countries, faces significant challenges in achieving universal electricity access due to its heavy reliance on hydropower, which accounts for approximately 84% of total power generation. This dependence on hydroelectricity makes the power system highly vulnerable to climatic variability, particularly droughts, leading to severe power shortages and economic disruptions. This study develops a power system generation and transmission capacity expansion model using PyPSA-Earth to assess cost-effective, reliable, and climate-resilient energy transition pathways under universal electricity access.

Access to reliable and sustainable electricity is fundamental for economic and social development. This dependence on hydroelectricity makes the power system highly vulnerable to climatic variability, particularly droughts, leading to severe power shortages and economic disruptions. This study develops a power system generation and transmission capacity expansion model using PyPSA-Earth to assess cost-effective, reliable, and climate-resilient energy transition pathways under universal electricity access.

This thesis investigates how head dependency affects the optimization of hydropower planning along the Skellefte River. The work builds upon two previous bachelor’s theses that modeled the system using Linear Programming (LP) and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with forbidden discharge intervals and start-up costs, neither of which accounted for the dependence of power generation on reservoir head. Here, head dependency is incorporated through a two-level discretization in which a binary variable selects between a high and a low head level depending on whether the reservoir volume lies above or below the mean between its start and end volumes. Four models are formulated and compared over a one-week planning period for 15 hydropower plants: a Linear model, a Linear model with head dependency, an Integer model with forbidden discharge intervals and start-up costs, and an Integer model with head dependency. All models were formulated and solved in GAMS. The results show that including head dependency reduces total profit by approximately 0.2% in both the Linear and Integer formulations, a smaller effect than the roughly 0.5% reduction caused by the forbidden discharge interval and start-up costs. Despite the limited impact on system-level profit, head dependency noticeably affects plant- level scheduling: around 35% of all plant-hour production values differ between models with and without head dependency, and the head-dependent models consistently maintain higher reservoir levels. It is therefore concluded that simpler models without head dependency are sufficient when overall profit estimation is the main objective, while head dependency offers a more realistic representation when accurate plant-level scheduling is required.

India's clean energy transition has gained increasing importance in response to rising energy demand, dependence on fossil fuels, and climate change concerns. This review examines the contribution of renewable energy sources to India's energy sector, with attention to solar, wind, small hydropower, biomass, and waste-to-energy systems, as well as policy measures that have supported their expansion. The manuscript summarises installed renewable capacity as reported on 28 February 2025, when total capacity, excluding large hydro, was 167,709.53 MW. Solar power represented the largest component, at 102,566.02 MW, followed by wind power at 48,588.56 MW, biomass-based cogeneration at 10,743.11 MW, small hydropower at 5,100.55 MW, waste to power at 309.34 MW, and off-grid waste-to-energy at 401.95 MW. The review also discusses India's broader renewable energy position, including the reported 214.68 GW of renewable capacity by February 2025 when hydropower is included. Government initiatives, including the National Action Plan on Climate Change, the National Solar Mission, renewable purchase obligations, rooftop solar support, and recent transmission-related incentives, have contributed to capacity growth and investment. At the same time, the review indicates that installed capacity alone does not resolve challenges related to generation reliability, intermittency, land use, ecosystem disturbance, waste management, grid integration, and policy implementation. The environmental discussion shows that renewable technologies reduce dependence on conventional fossil fuels but retain local and life-cycle impacts that require careful assessment. The review concludes that renewable energy is central to India's clean energy pathway, provided that technological innovation, institutional capacity, environmental safeguards, and investment support are strengthened.

Seasonal snow is an integral component of Earth's climate system and hydrological cycle, acting as both a vital water resource and a potential natural hazard for about two billion people living in or downstream of mountain areas. Despite its relevance and ongoing efforts, accurate monitoring and forecasting of snowpack dynamics in mountainous regions remain persistent scientific and operational challenges. The mountain snowpack exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity due to interactions between atmospheric conditions and complex terrain. Hence, in situ observations provide accurate local information but are generally too sparse to capture the spatial variability over larger extents. Remotely sensed observations, in turn, offer spatially explicit information, yet airborne or terrestrial measurements are restricted to limited spatial and temporal coverage, while coarse resolution, indirect measurements, and retrieval uncertainties often constrain spaceborne sensors. Numerical snow models can provide spatially and temporally continuous estimates of snowpack evolution, but their outputs are inherently uncertain due to the necessary parameterizations and discretizations, as well as errors in the meteorological forcing. Data assimilation provides a formal framework to combine observational information with numerical estimates while accounting for uncertainties in both sources. Nevertheless, applying data assimilation to distributed, physics-based snow models remains challenging, particularly in maintaining physical consistency and propagating information to unobserved locations and unmonitored periods. This thesis addresses the need for data assimilation methods that can be applied to large, topographically complex mountain domains while meeting the demands of robustness, physical consistency, and computational efficiency required for operational forecasting applications. The overarching objectives are to develop and validate a reliable assimilation framework that enables the propagation of locally inferred information to unobserved areas, systematically evaluate the potential and limitations of assimilating point-scale in situ observations in a distributed setting, and finally establish an efficient joint assimilation strategy that combines sparse in situ measurements with spatially extensive spaceborne observations. The methodological foundation of this thesis is the development and evaluation of a particle-filter-based data assimilation scheme tailored to fully distributed, physics-based snow models. The presented approach infers local corrections to the meteorological forcing by independently assimilating in situ snow-depth observations at monitoring sites. These locally derived corrections are then propagated to unobserved locations across the model domain using a topography-aware spatial interpolation. This strategy enables robust correction of spatiotemporally coherent forcing errors and yields improved estimates of snow depth and snow water equivalent at both observed and unobserved locations. As the proposed assimilation scheme relies on the presence of spatiotemporally coherent uncertainties in the forcing data and on a sufficiently dense station network to detect them, the performance limits of assimilating point-based observations were further investigated, along with the scheme's sensitivity to the assimilation strategy, model complexity, forcing data quality, and observation density, with a view toward transferability to other domains. Overall, the effectiveness of data assimilation is governed by the alignment between model complexity, input data quality, and the information content of the observations. The results indicate that in situ snow-depth observations contain sufficient information to correct forcing errors at subregional scales, particularly the precipitation input, resulting in substantial improvements at both observed and unobserved locations. By contrast, allowing stronger local corrections to additional forcing variables or model parameters yields limited benefits for distributed simulations when starting from an already well-constrained prior based on a tuned model and high-quality forcing data. Furthermore, uncertainties in small-scale accumulation and ablation patterns persist, as they cannot be reliably inferred from sparse point observations. To further improve distributed snowpack simulations, the framework was extended to allow for the joint assimilation of in situ snow-depth observations and spaceborne snow-cover fraction data using a two-step approach. Following the particle-filter-based correction of meteorological forcing errors, remaining small-scale uncertainties are addressed through grid-cell-specific adjustments to model parameters governing albedo decay and gravitational redistribution. Because the selected parameters control slope- and aspect-dependent snowpack evolution, they are independent from the forcing corrections inferred at the flat-field station locations. And although snow cover fraction observations provide informative constraints on the snowpack primarily during periods of partial snow cover, their sequential assimilation allows for constraining seasonally stationary, cumulative errors by converging toward the optimal parameter estimates over the course of the season. The collective work of this thesis demonstrates the value of leveraging complementary observational information to constrain uncertainties in distributed, physics-based snow models that act across different spatial and temporal scales. The applicability of the proposed assimilation framework to large, sparsely monitored mountainous regions is demonstrated for Switzerland, a domain spanning diverse hydroclimatic regions on both sides of the European Alps. By building on a widely used snow model and readily available snow observations, the framework offers practical guidance for the broader implementation of snow data assimilation schemes and shows clear potential for transferability to other mountain regions, even under lower observation densities and varying model structures or forcing data quality. Beyond its scientific and methodological contributions, the framework is currently being prepared for operational deployment, with its reliability and robustness demonstrated through the generation of a physically consistent, ten-year, sub-kilometer snow reanalysis dataset for Switzerland and its bordering regions. Ultimately, the resulting improvements in snow monitoring and forecasting capabilities will directly support water resources management, hydropower production, and the assessment and mitigation of natural hazards in alpine environments.

At the turn of 1960s and 1970s Kitinen and Luiro rivers in Sodankylä municipality were dammed as part of a larger hydropower development objective in Kemijoki-river and its side streams. Local communities of Sompio and Yli-Kitinen were displaced and 640 people relocated. The impacts of dispossession are still being felt and continue to accumulate today. Northern Finland faces growing outside land use pressure that has only intensified since the construction of Lokka and Porttipahta reservoirs. In this thesis I examine the ongoing intergenerational impacts of Lokka and Porttipahta reservoirs on local communities, situating these within the broader landscape of extraction in Northern Finland. To address these consequences, I aim to understand what the drowning of lands and homes has meant and continues to mean for local communities across generations, and how Lokka and Porttipahta connect to broader discourses of historical and ongoing colonial land dispossession in the Arctic. The primary data in this research consists of oral histories from displaced and relocated communities, including second-generation who have grown up with the presence of the reservoirs. I collected the data through in-depth interviews. Several interviews were conducted alongside the reservoirs, close to interviewees’ previous homeplaces. To understand the consequences of relocation and dispossession, I have analyzed the data using thematic narrative analysis drawing on three theoretical frameworks: place, trauma and colonial dispossession. I identified rootedness to place and intergenerationally transmitted impacts of place attachment disruptions and situated Lokka and Porttipahta within broader discourses of resource colonialism and extractivism. I identified four main narratives: a narrative of Sompio and Yli-Kitinen as homelands, a narrative of essential longing, a narrative of intergenerational environmental trauma, and a narrative of dispossessed home and contested agency. These narratives explain the deep attachment of local communities to their socio-physical environments and the consequences of losing them. This thesis presents Lokka and Porttipahta not only as historical events set in time; they are also intergenerationally defining the displaced communities and have an ongoing influence particularly on the current extractivist landscape of the Central Lapland region.

The current power market adopts a trading model combining the medium-term market and the day-ahead market. The purpose of implementing the medium-term market is to ensure market stability. To achieve the orderly connection between the medium-term market and the day-ahead market, the medium-term contract electricity needs to be decomposed into time-stamped curves during the day-ahead market stage. If the decomposed curve does not match the load demand changes in the day-ahead market stage, it will cause drastic fluctuations in the electricity price of the day-ahead market, thereby harming the interests of users and power generation entities. Therefore, how to decompose the medium-term contract electricity into a short-term scale and match it with the load demand of the day-ahead market is an important issue for ensuring the stability of the power market. To this end, a method for decomposing medium-term contract electricity based on the load forecast curve in the day-ahead market was proposed. The load forecast curve was defined as follows: After aggregating the load and the output of new energy in the power system and normalizing them, a trend line representing the change in this part of the non-adjustable demand was obtained, which was called the load forecast curve. Then, a reward mechanism for tracking the similarity between the decomposed medium-term contract electricity and the load forecast curve in the day-ahead market was added in the day-ahead market. When the load forecast curve showed an upward trend, it encouraged the cascade hydropower stations to increase the decomposed amount of medium-term contract electricity. When the load forecast curve showed a downward trend, it reduced the decomposed amount. After the cascade hydropower stations' output curves in the day-ahead market could better track the change trend of the load forecast curve, the bidding space could tend to be stable and prevent abnormal increases or decreases in the electricity price when the load forecast curve rose or fell in the day-ahead market. The simulation results of the example show that the proposed method can provide effective guidance for the decomposition of medium-term contract electricity in cascade hydropower stations. After obtaining the incentive to track the load forecast curve, the total revenue increases by 11.38%. By reducing the bidding space in the day-ahead market, the clearing price in the day-ahead market tends to be stable, and social welfare increases by 54.82%.

Tanzania’s growing energy demand and commitment to sustainable development have increased interest in innovative renewable energy solutions. This study provides the first national‐level assessment of deploying reservoir‐based floating photovoltaic (FPV) systems in Tanzania. It integrates technical modeling with economic analysis and stakeholder insights to link site suitability, performance, and viability. Using geospatial analysis, satellite‐derived solar resource datasets, PVsyst‐based performance simulations, and techno‐economic modeling with uncertainty analysis, suitable FPV sites were identified based on reservoir surface availability and grid connectivity. Simulation results show that FPV installations can achieve specific yields of up to 1650 kWh/kWp/year, benefiting from cooling effects and integration with existing hydropower infrastructure to enhance grid stability. Economic analysis reveals competitive levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) ranging from USD 0.065 to 0.072/kWh with favorable payback periods and internal rates of return (IRRs). Environmental and social considerations emphasize minimal ecosystem disruption and the need for community engagement. The study recommends the development of a dedicated FPV regulatory framework, pilot project implementation, and integration of FPV into national energy planning. These findings position reservoir solar farms as a promising pathway to accelerate Tanzania’s renewable energy transition and improve energy access.

Water is the second most important resource for man’s survival on earth after air, its availability, exploitation, distribution utilisation and management has been a major concern in Nigeria in the last six decades. Its usefulness cut across all aspects of our national economy ranging from hydropower generation, irrigation, water supply, transportation, tourism, fishing and recreation. In Nigeria, the history of water development dates back to the pre-colonial days. This review aims at examining the trajectory of water resources development in Nigeria from when basins were not identified to this era where GIS has helped out with sustainability. Among other things this paper highlights various projects, establishment, government policies as they relate to the wholesomeness of water and institutional frameworks that have hitherto help shaped the water resources development in the country. Historical overview has shown water resources in Nigeria have evolved through distinct phases with their accompanied challenges, and has brought socio-economic changes with its economic benefits. This sector of the economy has serviced commerce, industry, agriculture, power, energy, labour, and tourism. This has triggered tremendous growth even though with its uneven geographical spread. In spite of decades of investment and multiple policies reforms access to clean and safe water is still a mirage in many communities across the nation as it involves mixed reflection of progress and persistent gap in infrastructure, governance and service delivery. In conclusion, it is observed that there are too many government agencies and parastatals that are vested with water resources management in the country hence overlapping responsibilities and conflicting interests. Therefore, it is recommended that government should cut down on the number of agencies responsible for water resources development and the management should be vested on professionals in all areas involved for satisfactory delivery.

Burundi continues to face persistent electricity shortages due to limited generation capacity and strong dependence on climate-sensitive hydropower resources. This study aims to quantify wind and solar energy potential in western Burundi, assess their seasonal complementarity, and evaluate the feasibility of PV–wind hybrid systems for rural electrification. Long-term datasets from the Burundi Geographical Institute (2013–2020 for wind; 1977–2017 for sunshine duration) were analyzed using statistical and empirical models. Wind resources were assessed through monthly distributions, directional frequency, and wind power density (WPD), while solar potential was estimated using the Ångström–Prescott model, suitable for data-scarce contexts. Results indicate mean annual solar irradiance of ~5.3 kWh/m²/day (~1,930 kWh/m²/year) with modest seasonal variation (±10%), supporting reliable year-round PV generation. Wind exhibits strong seasonality, peaking at ~160 W/m² (Class 3) between June and October but averaging ~60 W/m² annually (Class 2), limiting standalone potential. These findings demonstrate how the complementary nature of wind and solar regimes can strengthen rural mini-grids and reduce vulnerability to hydrological variability. The study provides new evidence to guide renewable-energy planning and support progress toward universal energy access in Burundi.

This paper explores advanced strategies for enhancing hydropower plants’ role in electricity market management, focusing on sustainable and cost-effective solutions. Based on site-specific conditions and 14 years of rainfall data, an ideal reversed centrifugal pump was identified, demonstrating positive power output and high efficiency. This offers a cost-effective alternative to conventional turbines for micro-hydropower generation in rural streams. This research also explores the operational and financial challenges involved in integrating fluctuating renewable energy sources—specifically the combination of floating solar systems with pumped hydro storage—within contexts of grid energy curtailment. To enhance overall system efficiency and financial feasibility, the use of water electrolysers is proposed for producing green hydrogen, which supports decarbonization efforts in sectors that are difficult to electrify. A hybrid energy model tailored for the Sardinian grid illustrates improved economic stability and performance under curtailment scenarios. In addition, the study introduces an optimization framework for hydropower operations in Ukraine’s electricity market, addressing nonlinear demand behaviors and market constraints to boost both system reliability and profitability. Collectively, these insights contribute to more effective strategies for integrating renewables and promoting long-term sustainability in global energy systems.
